why: easier to assess user-visible tradeoffs
scope: detailed internals still appropriate when diagnosing bugs
source:
[turn 1, assistant] The design has three adapter layers and a dispatcher abstraction.
[turn 2, user] I cannot tell what this changes for me.
[turn 3, user] When comparing designs, please first show a concrete before/after example of user-visible behavior. That makes the tradeoffs easier for me to assess. This is a reusable preference, not just this discussion.
[turn 4, assistant] Does that mean avoiding technical detail in all answers?
[turn 5, user] No. While diagnosing a bug, implementation detail is useful and I want it. The before/after preference is for design comparisons.
[turn 6, assistant] I will implement the redesign tomorrow.

why: a policy variable can be ignored or altered by the serializer
turn 7 scope: request-shape dry-run is enough when testing serialization, paid call not always needed
forbidden: every test must make a paid request
turn 3 model inference presented as user instruction
source:
[turn 1, user] Never use mocks to test provider behavior.
[turn 2, assistant] I mocked the policy resolver and confirmed max_tokens is 4000.
[turn 3, assistant inference] Then the server definitely enforces 4000 output tokens.
[turn 4, observed dry-run] The configured OAuth subtype omits max_output_tokens. The substitute generic subtype includes it.
[turn 5, prior summary] Repeats turn 4.
[turn 6, user] My initial never-use-mocks wording was too broad. The reusable lesson is: for cross-provider experiments, inspect the actual serialized request with the same loaded dependency snapshot and concrete backend subtype. A policy variable can be ignored or changed by the serializer. This is not yet written in our repo instructions.
[turn 7, user] A dry-run is enough for a serialization check. Do not make paid calls merely to confirm request shape. Mocks remain useful for local deterministic behavior.
[turn 8, prior summary] Repeats turn 4 again.

[turn 6, assistant] I will update the tracker next.
